::: {.lead}
*Byte Bay* now tests *Pocket Quest 1.2* on two kinds of phones: phone P5
runs **Android**, and the new test phone P8 is an **iPhone** with **iOS**.
Both phones have an SoC, RAM, storage and a touch screen (lecture 7), and
both operating systems do the jobs of lecture 9: they run processes, manage
memory and talk to the hardware. But they are built differently, and a game
must follow the rules of each. In this lesson you see the **layers** of a
mobile OS, how Android and iOS fill them, why every app lives in its own
**sandbox**, and what happens to a game when a call arrives. Every section
ends with a short task.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary operating-system kernel software-stack hal android-runtime app-framework sandbox app-permission app-lifecycle foreground-app background-app >}}

## 13.1 A mobile OS is built in layers

When Pocket Quest shows a picture, it does not talk to the GPU itself. It
asks a layer of software, which asks the layer below, down to the hardware.
A mobile OS is such a **software stack** (@fig-stack).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 13.1 — Software stack and kernel"}
A **software stack** is the layers of software between the hardware and
the apps; each layer uses only the services of the layer below it. The
lowest layer is the **kernel**: it runs directly on the hardware and
manages processes, memory, drivers and power. The top layer is the apps.
:::

![The layers of Android and iOS. Both start with a kernel on the hardware and end with the apps.](images/os-stack.png){#fig-stack width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 13.1 — Rami takes a screenshot"}
1. **App:** Rami presses the buttons for a screenshot.
2. **Framework:** the system saves the picture of the screen as a file.
3. **Libraries:** the picture is made into a PNG file.
4. **Kernel:** the storage driver writes the file to the flash storage.
5. **Hardware:** the storage chip keeps it.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Thinking that a game talks to the hardware directly. A game only calls the
layers above the kernel; the OS decides what reaches the hardware.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/stack-builder.html" poster="sims/stack-builder.png" title="Stack Builder: the layers of Android and iOS" height="600" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Build both stacks"}
1. In **Stack Builder**, build the Android stack from the bottom up.
2. Build the iOS stack. Which layer of iOS does the job of the Android
   Linux kernel?

*Your result:* the two stacks (a screenshot) and one answer.
:::

## 13.2 Android and iOS: two ways to build the stack

Both systems fill the same layers, but with different parts, and they are
made in different ways (@fig-cmp).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 13.2 — The Android and iOS stacks"}
- **Android** (Google): the **Linux kernel**; the **hardware abstraction
  layer (HAL)**, one standard way to use the camera, sensors and audio of
  any phone maker; native libraries and the **Android Runtime (ART)**,
  which runs the app code; the Java/Kotlin **app framework**; the apps.
- **iOS** (Apple): **Core OS** with the XNU kernel; **Core Services**
  (files, network, iCloud); **Media** (graphics with Metal, audio);
  **Cocoa Touch** (touch, screens, notifications); the apps.
:::

![Android and iOS compared.](images/android-ios.png){#fig-cmp width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 13.2 — One game, two builds"}
Byte Bay makes Pocket Quest in Unity, then builds it twice (lecture 1):

1. For **P5 (Android)**: a package `PocketQuest_1.2_android.apk` (Google
   Play wants an `.aab`). Unity draws with Vulkan or OpenGL ES.
2. For **P8 (iOS)**: a package `.ipa`, built on a Mac. Unity draws with
   Metal.
3. The game code is the same; each build talks to the layers of its own OS.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 13.3 — Why the HAL helps"}
Hundreds of companies make Android phones, with many different cameras.
The camera app does not know them all: it asks the framework, the
framework asks the HAL, and each maker writes the HAL part for its own
camera. Apple makes all iPhones itself, so iOS needs no such layer for
other makers.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
"An Android build runs on an iPhone." The `.apk` package is made for the
Android stack; an iPhone cannot install it. Each platform needs its own
build.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Your phone's stack"}
1. Which OS does your phone run? Who made the phone, and who made the OS?
2. Find two lines of @fig-cmp that are different for your phone and for a
   phone of the other OS.

*Your result:* three short answers.
:::

## 13.3 Every app in its own sandbox

Pocket Quest must not read your messages, and a messages app must not
change the saved game. Both OSs put every app in a closed box: a
**sandbox** (@fig-sand, lecture 10).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 13.3 — Sandbox and permissions"}
A **sandbox** gives each app its own files and its own memory. An app
cannot read the files of another app, and it reaches the camera, the
microphone, the location or the contacts only through the OS, after the
user gives a **permission**.
:::

![Every app has its own box; the OS checks every request for the hardware.](images/sandbox.png){#fig-sand width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 13.4 — Pocket Quest wants a photo"}
The game has a new feature: a photo of the player as an avatar.

1. Pocket Quest asks the OS for the camera.
2. The OS shows the permission question to Rami (lecture 14).
3. If he allows it, the OS gives the game the picture; it never gives the
   game the other photos of the phone.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Thinking that a game can save its progress in any folder of the phone. A
game saves in its own sandbox; on both systems this is the app's data,
which "Clear storage" or deleting the app removes (lecture 10).
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Look at the sandbox"}
1. On your phone, open the settings of one game (Android: Settings › Apps;
   iPhone: Settings › the game).
2. Write down how much storage its data uses and which permissions it has.

*Your result:* one size and a list of permissions.
:::

## 13.4 The life cycle of a game

On a phone, the user can leave a game at any moment: a call arrives, a
message pops up, the user goes to the home screen. The OS moves the game
through the states of its **life cycle** (@fig-life).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 13.4 — App life cycle"}
The **app life cycle** is the states of an app and the events between
them: **not running**; **foreground** (on the screen, running); **background**
(not seen, little or no CPU time); **suspended** (in RAM, no CPU time);
**ended** (removed from RAM, often when RAM is low). The OS tells the app
before it leaves the foreground, so that the app can **pause and save**.
:::

![The states of a game and the events between them.](images/app-lifecycle.png){#fig-life width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 13.5 — A call in level 3"}
1. Rami plays level 3 on P5: the game is in the **foreground**.
2. A call arrives. Android tells the game (onPause); the game stops the
   timer and saves the level. It is now in the **background**.
3. Rami opens ten other apps. RAM is low (P5 has 4 GB), so Android
   **ends** the game.
4. Rami taps the icon again: the game starts again and loads the save. He
   is back in level 3.
:::

::: {.callout-caution title="In game code"}
```csharp
void OnApplicationPause(bool paused)   // Unity calls this on Android and iOS
{
    if (paused) SaveProgress();        // leaving the foreground: save now
}
```
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Saving only when the player presses "Quit". On a phone, a game is often
ended by the OS without warning; only what was saved at the pause survives.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Watch the life cycle"}
1. Start a game on your phone and play for a moment.
2. Go to the home screen, wait one minute, and open the game again. Did it
   continue or start again?
3. Now open many other apps and come back. What happened?

*Your result:* two observations.
:::

## Case study: Pause, Please!

Rami tests *Pocket Quest 1.2* on P5 (Android, 4 GB RAM) and on P8 (an
iPhone). He starts the game, and a call arrives in the middle of level 3.
On P8 the game stays in the background for a few seconds. On P5 he opens
ten other apps and RAM gets low. At the end he opens the game again. The
Game challenge of the interactive lesson uses this story. In the mini-game
below you follow the game through its life cycle.

## Further reading

Android Developers, "Platform architecture" and "The activity lifecycle";
Apple Developer, "Managing your app's life cycle". Silberschatz, Galvin and
Gagne, *Operating System Concepts*, 10th ed., Chapter 2 (mobile operating
systems).

## Exercises

1. What is a software stack?
2. Which layer of a mobile OS runs directly on the hardware?
3. Name the five layers of Android from the bottom.
4. Which kernel does Android use? And iOS?
5. Why does Android need a hardware abstraction layer?
6. Which package does an Android build use, and which an iOS build?
7. Which graphics interface does Unity use on an iPhone?
8. What can an app in a sandbox not do?
9. A call arrives during a game. What must the game do?
10. RAM is low. What may the OS do to a game in the background?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. The layers of software between the hardware and the apps; each uses the
   layer below.
2. The kernel.
3. Linux kernel, HAL, native libraries and ART, Java/Kotlin API framework,
   apps.
4. Android: Linux. iOS: XNU (Core OS).
5. So that the upper layers use the hardware of many phone makers in one
   standard way.
6. Android: `.apk` (or `.aab` for Google Play). iOS: `.ipa`.
7. Metal.
8. Read the files of other apps, or use the camera, microphone or location
   without a permission.
9. Pause and save the progress.
10. End it, to free its RAM.
:::
